analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the Senate's first day of the 115th Congress and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, the bill never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the law that bans oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and required the government to hold lease sales in the refuge's coastal plain — at least 300,000 acres in a first sale within a year, with a second sale 18 months later. It would have declared drilling "compatible" with the refuge's purpose, waived environmental review for the first lease sale, and barred the government from studying a no-drilling alternative. It also sent land to two Alaska Native corporations, created a small impact-aid fund for nearby communities, and required Native hiring efforts and project labor agreements.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain guaranteed access to federal leases in a refuge that has been closed to production since 1980. Alaska Native corporations (the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation and Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation) would receive land conveyances and drilling rights on their existing lands. North Slope communities would get an impact-aid fund capped at $28 million, and construction workers would benefit from a required project labor agreement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and Alaska Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, the provision that has prohibited oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and authorizes exploration, leasing, development, production, and transportation in the coastal plain.

Requires the first competitive lease sale of at least 300,000 acres within one year of enactment and a second sale within 18 months of the first, so industry access would not depend on future administrative discretion.

Declares the leasing program and all drilling activities compatible with the refuge's founding purposes by statute, with no further findings required, and exempts the first lease sale from review under the National Environmental Policy Act.

Conveys surface land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and remaining subsurface land to the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, and authorizes drilling on those corporations' private lands inside the refuge area.

Creates a Coastal Plain Local Government Impact Aid Assistance Fund (capped at $28 million) for North Slope Borough, Kaktovik, and other affected Alaska communities, requires lessees to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives, and requires negotiation of project labor agreements covering construction and production work.

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which holds the refuge in trust. The coastal plain — calving ground for the porcupine caribou herd and habitat for migratory birds — would be opened to industrial development, and the bill itself would limit the environmental review that could weigh those risks. The public would receive royalties of at least 12.5% of production value, but the permanent change to a protected refuge could not be undone.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through a protected refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill rigs the review process in advance: it exempts the first lease sale from environmental review under NEPA and, for the second sale, forbids the Secretary from even identifying or analyzing a no-leasing alternative — so the question of whether drilling should happen at all could never be weighed.

Its wildlife protections are qualified at every turn: the 'no significant adverse effect' standard applies only 'to the maximum extent practicable,' and closures to protect caribou calving areas would be limited — 'necessary' closures in the deformed area and seasonal-only closures in the undeformed area.

By statute, it deems the entire leasing program compatible with the purposes of a national wildlife refuge, removing the compatibility review the Refuge System normally requires, while the local impact aid is capped at $28 million total — small against the scale of development authorized.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine benefits — impact aid for a handful of small Alaska communities, land conveyances to Native corporations, and union project labor agreements — are narrow and local. The main effect is a one-way, essentially irreversible change: guaranteed lease sales in the most biologically sensitive part of a national wildlife refuge, with the environmental review stripped down so that a no-drilling option could not even be studied. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that a bill that both mandates drilling and forbids analysis of the alternative is not a balanced weighing of the public's interest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy Committee on day one of the Congress, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced the bill on January 5, 2017, the first working day of the new Congress, with Senator Dan Sullivan as cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
That was the last action ever taken: the bill appears in the record with no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who wanted the refuge protected: with the bill dead, the statutory ban on oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain remained in force for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who wanted the refuge protected

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress; the committee she chaired never scheduled a markup or vote on it

for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction

against.what_they_did: Opposed opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to drilling throughout the period

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republican senators sponsored the bill, and because it never reached a hearing or a vote, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill hands the industry guaranteed, fast-tracked access to federal leases in a refuge closed to production since 1980, with mandated sale dates and waivable environmental review. The public would receive at least a 12.5% royalty on production, but bears the environmental risk and the permanent loss of a protected area.

industries.industry: Alaska Native regional and village corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill clears title and conveys surface and subsurface land to these corporations, authorizes drilling on their private inholdings, requires Native hiring efforts, and funds local impact aid. Their fortunes rise or fall with coastal plain development.
Every lease would carry a requirement to negotiate a project labor agreement for construction, maintenance, and production work, giving union labor a role in any build-out.

Industrial development in the refuge's coastal plain would degrade one of the country's most remote wild areas; the bill's 2,000-acre surface-disturbance cap limits but does not eliminate the footprint, which would be scattered across the plain.
